{"id": "19:49/q08", "question": "Who is included in 'each' whom God made a prophet?", "turns_on": "The antecedent of kull may be the immediately named pair, the sons collectively, or Abraham together with Isaac and Jacob.", "positions": [{"id": "19:49/q08/p1", "position": "Isaac and Jacob are each meant.", "reasons": "Baghawi, Tabarsi, Nasafi, Biqai and Tabatabai expressly name the two. {"id": "19:49/q10", "question": "Was Jacob a prophet during Abraham's lifetime?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "19:49/q10/p1", "position": "Yes; Jacob's prophethood and the prophetic succession were a joy Abraham could witness.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir argues that naming Jacob rather than his also-prophetic son Joseph requires Jacob's prophethood within Abraham's life. {"id": "19:49/q11", "question": "What general lesson does Abraham's loss and divine gift teach?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "19:49/q11/p1", "position": "Giving up people or worldly means for God brings a better divine replacement and no ultimate loss.", "reasons": "Kashshaf applies this to leaving unbelieving, wicked people and receiving believing prophetic children. Jishumi calls the rise in status God's custom; Nasafi specifies believing prophetic children in exchange for wicked unbelievers."}]}
{"id": "19:49/q12", "question": "How do spiritual readings extend the pattern of separation and reward?", "turns_on": "The reported analogies differ in whether the recompense is described as inner understanding or as gifts and assurances granted to other prophets.", "positions": [{"id": "19:49/q12/p1", "position": "Divine recompense is proportioned to spiritual struggle and may be inner understanding.", "reasons": "Al-Wasiti, reported by Sulami, speaks of leaders receiving understanding of recitation in legal rulings and of spiritual truth in afflictions. {"id": "19:49/q13", "question": "What other rewards to Abraham illustrate this divine pattern?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "19:49/q13/p1", "position": "Several episodes of Abraham's service received corresponding divine honors.", "reasons": "Razi says disavowing his father brought the title father of the Muslims (9:114; 22:78); laying down his son for sacrifice brought a great ransom (37:103,107); surrender to God brought a cool, safe fire (2:131; 21:69); care and prayer for this community brought inclusion in the five daily prayers (2:129); faithfulness concerning Sarah brought a blessed prayer place at his footprint (53:37; 2:125); opposition to creatures brought divine friendship (26:77; 4:125). He calls messengership requiring people's obedience a supreme worldly and afterlife blessing."}]}
{"id": "19:49/q14", "question": "How is Abraham's account used within the sūra's argument?", "turns_on": "The notes give two related roles for the account: correcting religious claims about Abraham and placing miraculous births in the sūra's sequence.", "positions": [{"id": "19:49/q14/p1", "position": "It presents the earlier prophets as teaching Muhammad's message and Abraham's true religion, addressing Christians and warning Quraysh.", "reasons": "Islahi says Quraysh's current religion differs from Abraham's and Ishmael's. {"id": "19:49/q15", "question": "How is Abraham's disavowal connected with divine guidance and dominion?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "19:49/q15/p1", "position": "Vision of God's dominion involves trials, and guidance follows disavowal by God's gift.", "reasons": "Burhan links this with the saying that disbelief's head is East and cites Abraham's declaration in 37:99 together with 19:49."}]}
{"id": "19:49/q16", "question": "What might the following gift of mercy to Isaac and Jacob mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "19:49/q16/p1", "position": "It may refer to imamate.", "reasons": "Tabatabai links the following gift of mercy with the account of Isaac and Jacob in 21:72–73."}]}
{"id": "19:97/q01", "question": "How does the opening fa connect this verse to its context?", "turns_on": "Whether the fa explains the duty to convey the revelation or branches from the preceding judgment and promise.", "positions": [{"id": "19:97/q01/p1", "position": "It follows a direction to convey the revelation and states how its good news and warning can be delivered.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshaf calls this the sura's concluding charge; al-Alusi connects the fa to delivery of the revealed sura; Ibn Ashur says it may explain the duty to speak despite the polytheists' anger and their offer to follow if criticism of their gods and ancestors ceased; Bursevi also places it in the context of conveying revelation."}, {"id": "19:97/q01/p2", "position": "It follows the judgment and promise in 19:94–96.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur relates the resulting warning to the obstinate and the good news to believers."}]}
{"id": "19:97/q02", "question": "What does the pronoun in yassarnahu refer to, and why is its antecedent unspoken?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "19:97/q02/p1", "position": "It refers to the Qur'an, understood without an explicit preceding name.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya compares the unspoken antecedent to the sun in 38:32; Ibn Ashur also cites 38:32 and compares the Qur'an's ease in 54:32. Kashshaf, Ibn Atiyya, Baydawi, Nasafi, Abu Hayyan, Ibn Kathir, Biqai, Bursevi, and Bint al-Shati stress clear or eloquent Arabic. Ibn Ashur says Arabic's excellence and ease of recitation aid distinction and memory, citing 26:192–95; Asad says divine speech is made accessible through human language and concepts, citing 14:4, 2:97, and 26:193–94. Tabatabai prefers Arabic rendering because it serves both purposes and fits the sura; he invokes 43:2–4 for a prior lofty reality. Study Quran cites 44:58 for the Prophet's and Companions' native Arabic; 54:17,22,32,40 describe ease of remembering. Damghani defines taysir generally as facilitation, including the Qur'an and an easy outcome."}, {"id": "19:97/q03/p2", "position": "He facilitated the Prophet's recitation and made the Qur'an flow on his tongue.", "reasons": "Tabari explains ease of Muhammad's r

{"id": "19:97/q05", "question": "How does the preposition in 'bi-lisanika' work grammatically?", "turns_on": "The preposition's sense and whether it attaches to an understood state, an implied sending down, or the act of making easy.", "positions": [{"id": "19:97/q05/p1", "position": "It locates the revelation in the Prophet's language and may form a circumstantial phrase.", "reasons": "Nasafi calls it a circumstantial phrase. {"id": "19:97/q07", "question": "What variant is reported for 'litubashshira,' and what difference does it make?", "turns_on": "Presence or absence of the doubled shin and the resulting intensity of the announcement.", "positions": [{"id": "19:97/q07/p1", "position": "Form I tabshura, without the doubled shin, conveys plain informing.", "reasons": "Qiraat ER contrasts it with the written Form II tubashshira, which carries solemn heralding."}, {"id": "19:97/q07/p2", "position": "Form II tubashshira conveys solemn heralding.", "reasons": "Qiraat ER contrasts its doubled shin with Form I's simpler informing."}]}
{"id": "19:97/q08", "question": "To whom are the glad tidings addressed, and what makes them God-fearing?", "turns_on": "Whether the recipients already observe piety, are brought to it by the Qur'an, or are distinguished by graded forms of avoidance.", "positions": [{"id": "19:97/q08/p1", "position": "Believers who obey, respond to revelation, and guard against disobedience.", "reasons": "Yahya calls them God-fearing; Wahidi defines them through obedience to the Prophet; Baghawi and Nasafi call them pious believers, and Ibn Kathir calls them responsive. {"id": "19:97/q16", "question": "What does the opponents' contentiousness show about the Qur'an's inimitability?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "19:97/q16/p1", "position": "Their failure to meet the Qur'anic challenge despite skill and incentive demonstrates inability.", "reasons": "Khattabi says scholars differ over the precise mechanism of inimitability but human inability is plain. {"id": "19:97/q19", "question": "How does this verse conclude Maryam and connect with neighboring suras?", "turns_on": "These are complementary observations about the sura's ending, the next sura, and the Arabic-letter openings.", "positions": [{"id": "19:97/q19/p1", "position": "It closes Maryam by summarizing the revelation's stories, lessons, promises, warnings, and purpose.", "reasons": "Kashshaf calls it the conclusion's instruction to relay revelation. {"id": "19:97/q21", "question": "How does the warning here lead into the destruction mentioned in the next verse?", "turns_on": "Whether the next verse stresses complete destruction with no surviving sight or sound, or disappearance from human report.", "positions": [{"id": "19:97/q21/p1", "position": "The next verse threatens the obstinate with the disappearance of peoples destroyed before them.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya says God rebuts their boast of argumentative strength with former peoples' destruction. sons": "Abu Hayyan relates the derivation to words for the senses and perceptible things."}, {"id": "19:97/q22/p4", "position": "Hanzala reads 'aw tusmaʿu' passively, 'or is heard'.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan reports Hanzala's reading of the next verse."}, {"id": "19:97/q22/p5", "position": "Rakz is a faint sound, an indistinct sound, or sound and perception.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba says it is sound that cannot be understood; Ibn Abbas in Abu Hayyan says a faint, quiet sound; Ibn Zayd broadens it to sound or perception."}]}

{"id": "20:2/q05", "question": "What does the lām and its construction express?", "turns_on": "How the purpose lām and any omitted preposition govern their complements; whether toil can syntactically lead to the later reminder.", "positions": [{"id": "20:2/q05/p1", "position": "The lām expresses the denied purpose: revelation was not sent in order to make him suffer.", "reasons": "Ibn Kaysān calls it the lām of lowering; Abū Ḥayyān notes its shift from God as sender to the Messenger as addressee. {"id": "20:2/q06", "question": "What does tashqā mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether the word denotes immediate fatigue or the broader state of misery opposed to happiness; several sources allow both.", "positions": [{"id": "20:2/q06/p1", "position": "It means to toil, tire, or reach exhaustion through effort.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī defines exhaustion at the limit of effort; al-Dāmghānī compares 20:117 and 20:123; al-Baghawī calls toil its basic sense; al-Bayḍāwī, al-Samīn and Bursevī cite the proverb about labor training a colt; al-Ālūsī adds a poem contrasting suffering rational and ignorant persons. {"id": "20:2/q07", "question": "What hardship does the verse relieve?", "turns_on": "Whether shaqāʾ addresses bodily toil in worship, emotional distress and responsibility for rejection, opponents' taunt, worldly humiliation, or enduring hardship.", "positions": [{"id": "20:2/q07/p1", "position": "Excessive night prayer and severe worship should not exhaust the Prophet.", "reasons": "Mujāhid compares 73:20 and ropes tied during prayer; al-Zajjāj and Abū Isḥāq mention one-legged prayer; al-Kalbī says the Prophet later divided night between prayer and sleep. Other accounts describe swollen feet, standing on toes, shifting weight, or all-night vigil. Al-Bursevī and al-Ālūsī invoke the easy, upright religion. Ibn ʿAṭāʾ adds that grateful service gives gnostics repose and cites the Prophet's grateful-servant reply. Al-Qāḍī objects that commanded worship would be happiness, not denied hardship."}, {"id": "20:2/q07/p2", "position": "He should not grieve, strain in debate, or blame himself for people's refusal to believe; his duty is to convey and remind.", "reasons": "Abū Muslim cites 18:6 and 4:80; others compare 18:6, 10:65, 88:22 and 6:107. Al-Qāshānī attributes rejection to hard veils and lack of receptivity, not faulty guidance. Al-Biqāʿī ties his fear to Quraysh's resistance and the prospect of long labor. Iṣlāḥī says the Prophet feared his own effort inadequate; the reminder serves receptive God-fearing people."}, {"id": "20:2/q07/p3", "position": "The verse refutes unbelievers who claimed that revelation or leaving their religion made him wretched.", "reasons": "Muqātil names Abū Jahl, al-Walīd, al-Naḍr and al-Muṭʿim; other transmitters name smaller groups or Quraysh generally. Al-Ḥasan says God answered their accusation, and al-Ṭabrisī says the Quran instead prepares and honors him in both lives. Al-Ālūsī sees rhetorical reuse of their word shaqāʾ."}, {"id": "20:2/q07/p4", "position": "He will not remain humiliated under hostile Meccan power; revelation promises later honor and strength.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī relates this to an early Meccan sūra and enemy dominance. Kur'an Yolu reports later power, prestige and recognition."}, {"id": "20:2/q07/p5", "position": "The faithful follower is relieved from ultimate hardship, especially in the afterlife.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī says adherence prevents suffering; some connect relief to abrogation of night prayer, while al-Ḥasan and Abū ʿAlī make it broad relief from afterlife hardship."}]}
{"id": "20:2/q08", "question": "For what benefit was the Qur'an sent?", "turns_on": "Whether the benefit is chiefly guidance for hearers, the Prophet's nearness and gratitude, or the happiness radiating through his character.", "positions": [{"id": "20:2/q08/p1", "position": "It is a reminder and guide for those who fear God, bringing mercy, light and happiness.", "reasons": "Muqātil contrasts suffering with reminder from the Creator of earth and seven heavens; Qatāda calls it mercy, light and a guide to Paradise. Al-Jishumī notes happiness through conveying and practicing it. Ibn Kathīr cites the Bukhārī-Muslim report that God gives religious understanding to one intended for good and a graded-good report from Thalaba about forgiving scholars; Thalaba is identified as al-Laythī, resident of Basra then Kufa, narrated by Samāk. Elmalılı adduces reports of angels descending for Usayd's recitation, the Prophet's exhortation at the Farewell Pilgrimage to hold to Qur'an, and fear of God marking the best reciter, then prays for illuminated hearts. Kur'an Yolu says revelation guides, reminds and warns responsible people without extinguishing life's joy."}, {"id": "20:2/q08/p2", "position": "It opens nearness and grateful service rather than imposing suffering.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭāʾ explains intense worship as gratitude for nearness and communion, citing the Prophet's grateful-servant reply. Al-Qushayrī says the Quran prepares the ground for connection and nearness."}, {"id": "20:2/q08/p3", "position": "It makes the Prophet happy through embodying its character and spreads happiness through him.", "reasons": "The Taʾwīlāt Najmiyya says his noble character gladdens inhabitants of heaven and earth."}]}

ording to the reports?", "turns_on": "The reports differ in speakers and named opponents, and in whether the triggering toil was all-night prayer, ropes, swollen feet, one-foot standing, toes, or shifting weight.", "positions": [{"id": "20:2/q09/p1", "position": "Four named Quraysh leaders mocked Muhammad as wretched for abandoning his fathers' religion.", "reasons": "Muqātil names Abū Jahl, al-Walīd b. al-Mughīra, al-Naḍr b. al-Ḥārith and al-Muṭʿim b. ʿAdī; after the Prophet answered that he was sent as mercy they repeated the charge. {"id": "20:2/q10", "question": "How does the verse connect with its surrounding passages?", "turns_on": "Whether the main connection is Maryam's closing warning, parallel consolation elsewhere, or the following description of the revealer.", "positions": [{"id": "20:2/q10/p1", "position": "It answers the Prophet's grief after Maryam's warning about destroyed or corrupt generations and anticipates receptive hearers.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī cites 19:58-59 and 19:98; Ibn al-Zubayr says the preceding warning could alarm Muhammad. Al-Biqāʿī says the sūra assures him that patient gentleness will grow his community, mentioning 19:96, 10:65 and the following throne statement in 20:5; early Muslims were calmed and ʿUmar became a defender rather than the community being destroyed like Noah's and Hūd's peoples."}, {"id": "20:2/q10/p2", "position": "It parallels other reassurances that prophets need not consume themselves over rejection.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī, al-Bayḍāwī and others cite 18:6; al-Qushayrī connects the reaction to 15:88. {"id": "20:2/q11", "question": "What is the force of the exception after this denial?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:2/q11/p1", "position": "The following 'except' means 'rather': the Qur'an was sent as a reminder.", "reasons": "Al-Burhān treats the exception as corrective rather than a literal exception from causing suffering."}]}
{"id": "20:2/q12", "question": "What does Ṭā Hā mean in this opening?", "turns_on": "Whether the letters function as unexpanded opening letters, a vocative, an imperative, a symbol of felicity, or divine names; one note's gloss is missing.", "positions": [{"id": "20:2/q12/p1", "position": "It is disconnected introductory letters.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUbayda compares other sūra openings; al-Sāmarrāʾī says these openings commonly precede mention of Qur'an and the best-known account challenges Arabs to match speech made from their own letters, citing 2:2, 3:3, 7:2, 36:2, 50:1 and 38:1. {"id": "20:2/q13", "question": "How is Ṭā Hā pronounced?", "turns_on": "Whether the two sounds undergo imāla, partial imāla, or full opening, and whether Arabic phonology permits imāla here.", "positions": [{"id": "20:2/q13/p1", "position": "Abū ʿAmr and Abū Isḥāq incline hāʾ and open ṭāʾ.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī lists this recitation among the dialect forms that al-Thaʿlabī regards as correct and eloquent. {"id": "20:2/q15", "question": "What does the verse imply for a believer's practice and life?", "turns_on": "How the denial of hardship applies to practical limits in worship and to the broader quality of life.", "positions": [{"id": "20:2/q15/p1", "position": "Prayer and Qur'an recitation should stop when weariness prevents alertness or understanding.", "reasons": "Anas reports the Prophet telling a woman to sleep rather than rely on a rope to stay upright; another prophetic report says to sleep when night recitation becomes difficult."}, {"id": "20:2/q15/p2", "position": "Qur'anic discipline guides and enriches life without imposing disabling hardship.", "reasons": "Asad says ethical discipline deepens awareness of right and wrong; Kur'an Yolu says worship does not exceed capacity and revelation guides without extinguishing joy."}]}

{"id": "20:3/q01", "question": "How is 'except as a reminder' construed with the preceding clause?", "turns_on": "Whether illa is disconnected or connected, what governs tadhkiratan, and whether a reminder can substitute for suffering or coexist with another purpose clause.", "positions": [{"id": "20:3/q01/p1", "position": "The exception is disconnected: the Quran was sent as a reminder, rather than to cause the Prophet hardship.", "reasons": "Baydawi, Nasafi, al-Zamakhshari as reported by Abu Hayyan and al-Samin, al-Samin, Biqai, Bursevi, Alusi and Tabatabai read illa as 'but'; Biqai cites a poetic exception qualifying praise. Study Quran allows 'however' as a turn from verse 2. Baydawi and al-Zamakhshari reject substitution because reminder and misery differ in kind. Al-Samin disputes the Shaykh's grammatical explanation of that difference: al-Zamakhshari means al-Farisi's semantic objection. Bursevi makes the accusative a purpose of revelation under a disconnected exception and says two purposes require substitution or coordination."}, {"id": "20:3/q01/p2", "position": "An omitted verb of sending or reminding governs the accusative reminder.", "reasons": "Al-Farra and al-Mubarrad supply 'We sent it down'; al-Mubarrad compares ellipsis in 92:19-20. The Kufan grammarians, Ibn Atiyya, Jishumi, Tabrisi and al-Samin also supply a verb; al-Samin gives 'but We reminded' or 'you remind by it.' Tabrisi prefers this analysis and calls the exception disconnected. Alusi reports 'rather, We reminded you with a reminder.' Majaz gives this as one reordered construal."}, {"id": "20:3/q01/p3", "position": "Tadhkiratan is an accusative of purpose or a cognate verbal noun governed by the revelation.", "reasons": "Nahhas prefers a verbal noun or purpose object; Tabrisi calls it a purpose object, and al-Nahhas as reported by Qurtubi says the Quran was sent to remind, not burden. Al-Zamakhshari allows a purpose object alongside li-tashqa because the first purpose lacks the conditions for a bare accusative while the second meets them; Alusi says the grammatical relations differ and multiple purpose clauses need no coordination. Al-Samin argues multiple purposes are possible. Tabatabai calls tadhkira an active verbal noun and the purpose of sending. Baydawi reports an alternative purpose attached to Quran through an understood adjective. Alusi also reports a purpose object if li-tashqa describes Quran, but this requires an omitted relative construction and unusual definite article. Objections by Abu al-Baqa and Baydawi disallow two direct purposes; Alusi answers that no causal link is required, or that reminding entails toil. Ibn al-Munir objects that this makes hardship a cause of revelation and conflicts with consolation in 18:6; Alusi rejects the supposed conflict."}, {"id": "20:3/q01/p4", "position": "Tadhkiratan substitutes for the syntactic position of li-tashqa or its verb.", "reasons": "Basran grammarians, Abu Ishaq, Ibn Atiyya, al-Akhfash, al-Zajjaj and Burhan give the substitute analysis: the Quran was sent only as a reminder.
